@dobson4e [§2.3.4] describes checking a fitted model's adequacy
by examining residuals:
summaries of how far each observation falls from its fitted value.
In a generalized linear model the outcome variance usually changes with the mean,
so raw differences $y_i - \est{\mu}_i$ are not on a common scale;
dividing by an estimated standard deviation puts them on one.

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#def-pearson-residual-glm}
#### Pearson residual and Pearson chi-squared statistic

For a generalized linear model with variance function $V(\mu)$
(@def-natural-parameter)
and dispersion parameter $\phi = 1$,
the **Pearson residual** for observation $i$ is

$$
r_i \eqdef \frac{y_i - \est{\mu}_i}{\sqrt{V(\est{\mu}_i)}},
$$

and the **Pearson chi-squared statistic** is
$X^2 \eqdef \sum_{i=1}^n r_i^2$
[@dunn2018generalized, Chapters 7 and 8].
For a Poisson outcome, $V(\mu) = \mu$.
:::

::: notes
If the model is adequate and the fitted means are not too small,
$X^2$ is approximately chi-squared distributed with $n - p$ degrees of freedom,
where $p$ is the number of regression coefficients,
so $X^2 / (n - p)$ should be close to 1;
a ratio well above 1 suggests overdispersion
[@dunn2018generalized, Chapter 7].
The [count regression chapter](count-regression.qmd) returns to overdispersion.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-chronic-pearson}
#### Pearson residuals for the chronic medical conditions model

The town woman who reports 4 conditions has fitted mean
$\est{\mu}_i = \bar{y}_{\text{town}} = 37/26$
(@exm-chronic-mle),
so her Pearson residual is

$$
\ba
r_i
&= \frac{4 - 37/26}{\sqrt{37/26}}
&& \text{(Pearson residual with } V(\mu) = \mu \text{)}
\\
&\approx \frac{4 - 1.4231}{1.1929}
&& \text{(evaluate } 37/26 \text{ and its square root)}
\\
&\approx \frac{2.5769}{1.1929}
&& \text{(subtract)}
\\
&\approx 2.160
&& \text{(divide)}
\ea
$$

```{r}
#| label: chronic-pearson
r_pearson <- residuals(chronic_glm, type = "pearson")
x2 <- sum(r_pearson^2)
df_resid <- df.residual(chronic_glm)
```

@fig-chronic-pearson plots all 49 Pearson residuals.
The largest residual in absolute value is
`r round(max(abs(r_pearson)), 3)`,
and the Pearson chi-squared statistic is
$X^2 \approx$ `r round(x2, 2)`
on $49 - 2 =$ `r df_resid` residual degrees of freedom,
so $X^2 / 47 \approx$ `r round(x2 / df_resid, 3)`.
No residual is extreme,
and the ratio is below 1,
so the data show no sign of more variability than the Poisson model allows.

::: {#fig-chronic-pearson}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)
chronic$pearson <- r_pearson
ggplot(chronic, aes(x = residence, y = pearson)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0) +
  labs(x = "Residence", y = "Pearson residual") +
  theme_bw()
```

Pearson residuals from the Poisson model for the chronic medical conditions data,
by residence
